summary: Describes specifics for applying Signaling Compression to SIP, such as default minimum parameter values, state management, and issues over TCP. Implementations must also support the SIP and SDP static dictionary. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: How to shrink phone-call setup messages and the settings both sides must use.

subtitle: How to compress SIP messages with SigComp: minimum parameters, one compartment per registration, and rules for TCP.

tldr.problem: SigComp is application-agnostic, so it leaves out the details a specific protocol needs, and some of its minimum parameter values are too small for good SIP compression.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC binds SigComp to SIP: it raises minimum values such as the decompression memory to 8192 bytes, requires the SIP/SDP static dictionary, identifies peers with a sigcomp-id URN, and ties compartment lifetime to SIP registration.
tldr.outcome: Any SigComp implementation used with SIP must conform to this document and to RFC 3320. It updates RFC 3486 by no longer recommending stateless compression, and it is itself updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5049 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2007. It updates RFC 3486 and is itself updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: Binding SigComp to SIP
sections.content:
SigComp (RFC 3320) compresses messages from application protocols. Its main driver is compressing SIP (RFC 3261) messages, but it was designed to be application agnostic, which is called ANY/SigComp. Many application-dependent details were therefore left out of the base standard, with the expectation that a separate specification would describe them for each application protocol. This document is that specification for SIP, called SIP/SigComp.

Any SigComp implementation used to compress SIP messages MUST conform to this document and to RFC 3320. It must also support the SIP/SDP static dictionary from RFC 3485 and the mechanism for discovering SigComp support at the SIP layer from RFC 3486.
sections.eli5: SigComp is a general shorthand for any kind of message. This document fits the shorthand to phone-call setup messages.

sections.title: Minimum Parameter Values
sections.content:
RFC 3320 sets minimum values every SigComp endpoint must support, chosen with all imaginable devices in mind. Some are too small for good SIP compression, so SIP/SigComp raises them. They apply only to SIP/SigComp. An endpoint MAY offer more than the minimums.

Decompression memory size goes from 2048 to 8192 bytes. With 2048 bytes the compression ratio is seriously limited, and some messages cannot be compressed at all. This memory is needed only temporarily during decompression, so 8 KB should not trouble an endpoint that already implements SIP and SigComp. State memory size goes from 0 to 2048 bytes per compartment, so an endpoint can upload state in its first message without wondering whether the peer can store it. An endpoint MAY offer different values for different compartments, as long as none is below 2048.

Cycles per bit stays at 16. The SigComp version must be at least 0x02, meaning SigComp plus NACK, so a decompression failure produces a NACK to the compressor (RFC 4077) and the compressor can compress optimistically from the start. The minimum locally available state is the SIP/SDP static dictionary, which is mandatory and so need not be advertised.
sections.eli5: Both sides agree the shared notebook has to be a decent size, and that they must tell each other when a note cannot be read.

sections.title: Sharing a Port, TCP Streams and Retransmissions
sections.content:
To save ports, an endpoint may receive both SigComp messages and plain SIP messages on one port. On message transports such as UDP or SCTP, the receiver looks at the first octet of each payload. If its most significant bits are 11111 it is SigComp; any other value is taken to be an uncompressed SIP message. On a stream transport such as TCP the decision is made once per connection from the first octet of the stream. Applications MUST NOT mix SIP and SigComp messages on one TCP connection. If it carries SigComp, every message MUST have a SigComp header and be delimited with 0xFFFF. A sender that really needs both can use the null-decompression bytecodes in RFC 4896 to send uncompressed SIP that is still valid SigComp.

Continuous mode is not used with SIP/SigComp, because it needs transport-level protection against denial of service and TCP alone is not enough. SigComp cannot compress messages larger than 64k, so a larger SIP message MUST NOT be sent on that TCP connection and SHOULD go over a different one.

Retransmitted SIP messages MUST be compressed again, taking into account any SigComp state created or invalidated since. Implementations MUST NOT cache and resend the old compressed result, since the first copy may already have changed state that the cached bytes rely on.
sections.eli5: A receiver peeks at the first few bits of each message to tell shorthand from plain writing. When you resend a message you must rewrite the shorthand, because the notebook may have changed.

sections.title: Compartments and Remote Application Identifiers
sections.content:
A compartment holds the state needed to compress outgoing and decompress incoming messages for one remote application. To compress well, an application assigns distinct compartments to distinct remote applications.

Each SIP/SigComp application MUST have a persistent, globally unique URN as its SIP/SigComp identifier, and SHOULD use a UUID URN (RFC 4122). A device with a globally unique instance identifier SHOULD reuse it, which improves compression of headers carrying both. A server farm sharing state MUST use one identifier for all its servers. The identifier travels in the sigcomp-id parameter of a SIP URI or a Via header field, and an application that puts comp=sigcomp in a URI or its own Via entry MUST add it.

For matching: an outgoing request uses the identifier of the target URI, an incoming request the identifier in the top-most Via entry, and responses reuse the identifier of the request they belong to. If no identifier is present, the peer is identified by IP address and port for connectionless transports, or by the connection for connection-oriented ones, to support legacy implementations.

Compartment lifetime is linked to registration. A compressed REGISTER should open a compartment (for both the sender and the registrar or relaying proxy), and compartments are typically closed when the registration expires or is canceled. They MAY be closed on a non-2xx final response, but SHOULD NOT be closed before a successful registration is over. If a compartment already exists for that identifier, the application MUST reuse it. Earlier drafts also had transaction and dialog compartments, but they were dropped because the complexity, such as edge proxies keeping dialog state, outweighed the benefit.

Stateless compression is usually not worthwhile and may expand messages, so an application with no compartment MAY send uncompressed even when comp=sigcomp is present. This reverses the advice in RFC 3486 that the client SHOULD compress.
sections.eli5: Each pen pal gets their own notebook. The notebook is opened when you sign in, kept while you are signed in, and put away when you sign out.

sections.title: Network Setup, TLS and Compatibility
sections.content:
Network administrators can raise compression efficiency. It is RECOMMENDED that registrars be configured so proxies doing SigComp appear in both the Path and the Service-Route routes, and that those proxies put themselves into Record-Route so in-dialog requests follow. It is also RECOMMENDED that user agents stay registered while a dialog is active, because a closed compartment may leave later in-dialog requests uncompressed.

Compressing twice, once with SigComp and again with TLS compression, brings no significant gain. Because TLS could mostly compress only the SigComp code itself, using TLS compression together with SigComp is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Private agreements MAY deviate from the minimum values, continuous mode and the compartment definition if they say so unambiguously. For backward compatibility, the rules were designed to maximize interoperability with existing deployments, but legacy implementations may have a smaller decompression memory, no NACK support or a different compartment mapping.
sections.eli5: For shorthand to keep working, every helper on the path must be on the same notebook. Shrinking an already shrunk message again does not help.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3320 apply. The RFC adds that keeping SigComp state longer than a SIP dialog should not pose new security risks, because the state was allowed to be created in the first place.

IANA registered the sigcomp-id Via header field parameter and the sigcomp-id SIP URI parameter in the SIP Parameters registry, with no predefined values.
sections.eli5: The old safety rules still apply, and the new name tag was added to the official list so nobody else uses it.
